description: We are faculty of electronics students, who are in love with space! We want to expand educational opportunities, as well as create something useful for future space missions.
summary: We created an interactive 3D map of Mars, that map works as a survival guide. It shows conditions, key places and rovers, and plans routes that balance distance against steepness. The surface view and Detailed view let users inspect a site before choosing it, as terrain mistakes are costly for a crew far from Earth. The same tool also works as an interactive lesson for students.
details:
Mars Explorer lets a user move from a stylised Solar System to a detailed model of Mars. From there they can:

rotate the globe or switch to a flat map, and zoom in on a region;
change the Layout between natural colour, elevation, temperature, roughness, dust and other layers;

hide/unhide grid and labels on the surface;

explore any point of Mars surface by clicking Explorer button and choosing a place on the map; you can take a closer look by observing a detailed 3d model of key places by clicking Detailed view;

go to the simulations tab and view 3d simulations of marsquake, dust storm, Phobos and Deimos movement during the day as well as day-night cycle.

open the Markers panel, which has 4 subpanels:

routes, to help plan safest routes using elevation map and show according data;

vehicles, to show mars rovers position;

user marks, to mark a place, set its category, name and description;

places of interest, to show information on the key attractions of Mars surface.


The planet is drawn in the browser with WebGL. Colour and elevation come from tiles, which are small image pieces loaded only for the area in view.
The shaders turn elevation into relief, lighting and shadows. They also draw the highlight ring for a selected place, the route line and the A/B pins.
For a route, the program loads the elevation of the area around the two points and treats it as a grid of cells. It then searches for the cheapest path with the A* algorithm, where cost depends on distance, steepness and total climbing. There are three modes: Gentle, Balanced and Shortest.
The path is smoothed, and the program computes its length, ascent, descent, maximum and average slope, and the elevation profile. It also compares the route with a straight line, so the user sees what the detour buys them.

It turns raw NASA data into something people can read and use without special training.
Everything is in one place: terrain, conditions, places, surface view and route planning.
It needs no installation and runs in an ordinary browser.
The route is a trade-off rather than just the shortest line, which mirrors real decisions on Mars.

Our goal is Martian map that helps both future explorers and today’s learners. We want to bring astronauts’ real questions (where can we go, how hard is it, what will it be like there) into one tool. We also want to open that tool to schools, so that learning about Mars is an activity and not just reading. Next steps include adding more layers to the route cost (roughness, dust, temperature, hazards), higher-resolution elevation data, and ready-made classroom missions.


Technologies and programming languages.
JavaScript (ES modules) for the application logic.
GLSL for the shaders that draw the planet, the highlight rings and the routes.
HTML and CSS for the interface.
three.js (r128) on top of WebGL for 3D graphics.
Vite for development and building, with a build mode that produces a single standalone bundle.
Node.js with its built-in test runner for the automated tests.
Data. NASA Mars Trek map tiles (the Viking colour mosaic, MOLA elevation and TES layers). The route planner uses a local pyramid of MOLA elevation tiles that we host ourselves.
Hardware. There is no special hardware. It runs on a desktop, laptop, tablet or phone with a modern browser and a graphics chip that supports WebGL. A newer device gives smoother rendering of the detailed globe.
Software. Any modern browser (Chrome, Firefox, Edge or Safari) to use it. To build it, Node.js and Vite are needed. For testing we used Playwright with Chromium to check the interface and the shaders. For development we also used Claude, an AI assistant, to help write and review the code, so mention it if the challenge rules ask about AI tools.
Limits. The route planner currently uses elevation only, and the elevation data is coarse (about 1 to 40 km per pixel depending on the route length), so slopes are averaged. It is a prototype for learning and early planning, not an operational tool for a real mission.

Our project is creative, as we implemented a lot of interactivity, like weather simulations, high detailed 3d models, that feel like you aren't just looking on a screen, but exploring Mars on your own.

We considered accessibility of the project. We made sure that it doesn't need expensive hardware to run, you can run the project in any web browser from basically any device!
